title: Does the idempotent producer protect you from application-level duplicate publishes?
shortTitle: Does the idempotent producer protect you from application-level duplicate publishes?

s1_definition.profdef: No. The idempotent producer, enabled with `enable.idempotence=true`, only guarantees that the Kafka client's own internal retries do not create duplicates on the broker. It works by tagging each record with a producer id, an epoch, and a monotonically increasing per-partition sequence number, so the broker can detect and discard a retransmission of a record it already persisted. It does not deduplicate two logically distinct `send()` calls that your application code made, because those carry different sequence numbers and the broker treats them as two separate records. Application-level duplicates require an application-level idempotency key and a dedup check, not the idempotent producer.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh mails a transfer instruction to National Bank of India. The post office (the Kafka client) guarantees that if it has to resend the same sealed envelope because of a delivery hiccup, the bank will only process it once, because each envelope has a tracking number and the bank ignores a tracking number it already saw. That is the idempotent producer. But if Rajesh himself, worried the first letter was lost, writes a brand new letter asking for the same transfer and mails it, those are two different envelopes with two different tracking numbers, and the bank will happily process both, debiting him twice. Stopping that requires Rajesh to write his own reference number on the request and the bank to reject a reference it already honored. That is application-level idempotency.
s1_definition.oneliner: The idempotent producer deduplicates the client's retransmissions within one producer session, not two separate sends from your code — for application-level duplicates you need your own idempotency key and a dedup store.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** No. The idempotent producer, enabled with `enable.idempotence=true`, only guarantees that the Kafka client's own internal retries do not create duplicates on the broker. It works by tagging each record with a producer id, an epoch, and a monotonically increasing per-partition sequence number, so the broker can detect and discard a retransmission of a record it already persisted. It does not deduplicate two logically distinct `send()` calls that your application code made, because those carry different sequence numbers and the broker treats them as two separate records. Application-level duplicates require an application-level idempotency key and a dedup check, not the idempotent producer.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh mails a transfer instruction to National Bank of India. The post office (the Kafka client) guarantees that if it has to resend the same sealed envelope because of a delivery hiccup, the bank will only process it once, because each envelope has a tracking number and the bank ignores a tracking number it already saw. That is the idempotent producer. But if Rajesh himself, worried the first letter was lost, writes a brand new letter asking for the same transfer and mails it, those are two different envelopes with two different tracking numbers, and the bank will happily process both, debiting him twice. Stopping that requires Rajesh to write his own reference number on the request and the bank to reject a reference it already honored. That is application-level idempotency.

**One line to remember:** The idempotent producer deduplicates the client's retransmissions within one producer session, not two separate sends from your code — for application-level duplicates you need your own idempotency key and a dedup store.

sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India exposes a transfer API. When the API publishes a settlement event, it uses an idempotent producer because the team assumed that was enough to prevent double settlements. Rajesh (SAV2001) transfers to Priya (CUR3001).

Problem 1 — Rajesh's mobile app timed out waiting for the transfer response and automatically retried the HTTP request. The API handled both requests and called the publish method twice for the same transfer id. The idempotent producer did nothing to stop this, because these were two separate sends, so two settlement events landed and Priya was credited twice. This is exactly the limit of the idempotent producer: it only catches the client's own retransmissions.

Problem 2 — we needed a fix that works even across producer restarts and across multiple API instances. This is why the real fix lives at the consumer, using the transfer id as an idempotency key against a durable store.

Our runnable demo models an `IdempotentProducer` that dedupes only its own retransmissions by sequence number, shows that two application sends still produce two records, and then a `DedupConsumer` that uses a transfer id against a processed-keys store to apply the settlement exactly once. The classes are `DuplicateDemo`, `IdempotentProducer`, `Broker`, `SettlementEvent`, and `DedupConsumer`.

The SQL table that makes consumer-side dedup durable:

```sql
-- V1__create_dedup_tables.sql (Flyway migration)
CREATE TABLE processed_transfers (
    transfer_id  VARCHAR(40) PRIMARY KEY,         -- the idempotency key
    account_id   VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    amount       DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL,
    processed_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE TABLE account_balances (
    account_id   VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    balance      DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO account_balances (account_id, balance) VALUES
    ('SAV2001', 1000000.00),
    ('CUR3001', 250000.00);
```

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: kafka-1:9092,kafka-2:9092,kafka-3:9092
    producer:
      acks: all
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true     # dedupes CLIENT RETRIES only, NOT app duplicates
    consumer:
      group-id: settlement-apply
      enable-auto-commit: false
```

```bash
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run it
java -jar target/transfer-api-service-1.0.0.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/transfers \

  -H 'Idempotency-Key: TXF-123' \
  -d '{"from":"SAV2001","to":"CUR3001","amount":50000}'

# Run the demo (client retry vs app duplicate vs consumer dedup)
javac demo/DuplicateDemo.java -d out
java -cp out com.bank.transfer.demo.DuplicateDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one logical transfer with id TXF-123 crediting Priya fifty thousand, under three scenarios.

Step 1: The idempotent producer sends the settlement for TXF-123. The broker assigns it sequence zero for this producer id and partition and persists one record.

Step 2: The acknowledgment is lost, so the client retransmits the exact same batch with the same sequence zero. The broker sees a sequence it already accepted and discards the retransmission, so the record count stays at one. This is the idempotent producer doing its job against client retries.

Step 3: Now the mobile app retried the HTTP request, so the API called the publish method twice. The producer issues two sends with two different sequence numbers. The broker treats them as two distinct records and persists both. The record count is two, a duplicate settlement, and the idempotent producer did nothing, because these were not retransmissions of the same batch.

Step 4: The consumer reads both records. On the first, the transfer id TXF-123 is not in the processed store, so it credits Priya and records the id. On the second, TXF-123 is already present, so it skips the credit and acknowledges. Priya is credited exactly once.

Step 5: This dedup store is durable and shared, so it also protects against producer restarts and multiple API instances, which the in-session idempotent producer could never do, confirming the fix must live at the application and consumer level keyed by the business id.

Final output:

```

[2026-10-24 22:48:19] [INFO] Records on broker after client retry = 1 (idempotence collapsed the retransmission)

[2026-10-24 22:48:19] [INFO] === Consumer-side dedup by transferId fixes it ===
```

```
  Logical transfer TXF-123 -> credit Priya 50000
    │
    ├─ CLIENT RETRY (lost ack)                      ├─ APPLICATION DUPLICATE (HTTP retried)
    │  send(seq=0) -> broker stores                 │  send(seq=0) -> broker stores
    │  retransmit same batch(seq=0)                 │  send(seq=1) -> broker stores AGAIN
    │    │ broker: seq 0 already seen                │    │ broker: seq 1 is new
    │    ▼ DISCARD                                   │    ▼ WRITE (duplicate!)

    ▼                                               ▼
  no duplicate                                      DUPLICATE settlement
                                                     │

                                            TXF-123 seen before? skip credit

```

```
       │ no

  [APPLYING] ──credit + mark processed (one txn)──→ [APPLIED] (ack)

  1. API publish(TXF-123)   // twice due to HTTP retry
  2. broker stores 2 records (idempotent producer cannot tell they match)
  3. consumer.onSettlement(record#1): processedRepo.exists(TXF-123)? no
  4.   credit Priya; processedRepo.markProcessed(TXF-123)   // same DB txn

```
sections.s6_takeaway:
No, the idempotent producer does not protect you from application-level duplicate publishes, and understanding why is important. The idempotent producer, which you turn on with enable idempotence true, solves exactly one narrow problem: duplicates caused by the Kafka client's own retries. It tags every record batch with a producer id, an epoch, and a monotonically increasing per-partition sequence number, so if the producer resends a batch because an acknowledgment was lost, the broker recognizes the sequence number it already accepted and discards the retransmission. That removes duplicates from retries and also preserves ordering. But the sequence number is assigned by the client per send call, so if your application code calls send twice for the same business event, those are two different sequence numbers and the broker stores two separate records. The idempotent producer has no notion of business identity.

This is exactly the trap we hit on the National Bank of India transfer API. Rajesh's mobile app timed out and automatically retried the HTTP request, our API processed both requests and published the settlement twice for the same transfer id, and because these were two independent sends and not a client retransmission, both landed on the topic and Priya was credited twice. The idempotent producer was enabled the whole time and was powerless, because it only ever deduplicates the client's own retransmission of the same batch within a single producer session.

The correct fix is an application-level idempotency key combined with a durable dedup check, placed as close as possible to the side effect. Our events carry the transfer id as the idempotency key, and the consumer that actually applies the credit first checks a processed-transfers table with the transfer id as its primary key. If the id is already there, it skips the credit and acknowledges; if not, it credits the account and records the id in the same database transaction. Because that store is durable and shared across all consumer instances, it protects us even across producer restarts and multiple API pods, which the in-session idempotent producer could never do.

The mental model I give the team is a layered one. The idempotent producer handles the transport layer, meaning retries on the wire. Kafka transactions build on it to give atomic multi-partition writes and effectively-once consumption within Kafka, but even transactions do not know that two of your sends mean the same thing. Business-level exactly-once is your responsibility and lives in your idempotency key and dedup store, and when a publish must be exactly-once together with a database write, I reach for the transactional outbox pattern so there is a single source of truth for whether the event exists. In short, the idempotent producer is necessary but never sufficient for real-world duplicate prevention.
